candidates.attacker_control: The HTTP request body and the effective content type are both attacker-controlled. `Request.getBody()` unconditionally returns the raw request body (Request.java:409-427) and even allows a form POST to smuggle an arbitrary body/type pair via the `_content` and `_content_type` parameters, while `Request.getContentType()` selects the engine from the raw Content-Type header (or the Accept header / URI suffix, Request.java:318-322, 386-400). Sending `application/x-yaml` (or `_content_type=application/x-yaml` on a form POST, or a missing Content-Type plus an `application/x-yaml` accept type) routes the attacker's text straight into SnakeYamlEngine.fromString, where the YAML parser honours attacker-chosen global tags.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked (a) whether the module is required: `pippo/pom.xml` bundles only pippo-core, pippo-jetty, pippo-freemarker and pippo-gson, so the finding is scoped to applications that opt into pippo-snakeyaml; (b) whether the fix exists elsewhere: XStream (XstreamEngine.java:42-56) and Java serialization of session data (SerializationSessionDataTranscoder.java:48-56 with WhitelistObjectInputStream) were explicitly hardened in this same unreleased cycle (CHANGELOG.md:8-9, issues #454/#458), while the SnakeYAML engine has no such restriction, and FastJSON was bumped to 1.2.51 — the asymmetry indicates body deserialization is treated as untrusted elsewhere; (c) whether an engine registered earlier could shadow it: possible only if another engine claims `application/x-yaml` first, which requires the optional jackson-dataformat-yaml dependency or custom registration; (d) whether the exception handling in Request.createEntityFromBody mitigates it: no, instantiation happens before the cast/exception; (e) the serialization direction (`toString`/`dump`, line 43) is not the issue.
candidates.impact: Deserialization of untrusted data with arbitrary class instantiation in the application's JVM, under the application's privileges: at minimum memory/state manipulation and denial of service, and — with commonly available gadget classes or remote class loading — remote code execution. An internet-facing application that includes pippo-snakeyaml and parses request bodies is exposed with no authentication beyond whatever the endpoint itself enforces.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application has the optional `pippo-snakeyaml` artifact on its classpath (so SnakeYamlInitializer registers SnakeYamlEngine for `application/x-yaml`; it is not part of the default `pippo` aggregate bundle). 2) No other YAML engine was registered first for that content type — e.g. Jackson's YAML engine requires the optional `jackson-dataformat-yaml` dependency, and `ContentTypeEngines.registerContentTypeEngine` silently ignores a later duplicate (ContentTypeEngines.java:98-105). 3) At least one endpoint deserializes the request body, e.g. a controller method parameter annotated `@Body` (BodyExtractor.java:38-48) or application code calling `routeContext.createEntityFromBody(...)` / `Request.createEntityFromBody(...)`. 4) Exploitation depth depends on which gadget-compatible classes/URL-loading capabilities exist in the application's runtime classpath.
candidates.root_cause: SnakeYamlEngine.fromString parses attacker-supplied request-body text with SnakeYAML's default (non-restricted) API: `return (T) new Yaml().load(content);` (SnakeYamlEngine.java:46-49). The default `Yaml()`/`Constructor` path of the pinned SnakeYAML 1.17 (pippo-snakeyaml/pom.xml:17-33, `<snakeyaml.version>1.17</snakeyaml.version>`) resolves and instantiates arbitrary Java classes named by global YAML type tags instead of being limited to plain data types (no `SafeConstructor`, no `LoaderOptions`/type restrictions, and no result-type filter on `classOfT`). The engine is auto-registered for `application/x-yaml` (and suffix `yaml`) by SnakeYamlInitializer.init (SnakeYamlInitializer.java:28-31) through the `@MetaInfServices`/ServiceLoader mechanism consumed in Application.init (Application.java:99-109), so any application that has this optional module on the classpath exposes an unsafe deserializer through the framework's normal body-parsing API.
candidates.title: Unsafe YAML deserialization in SnakeYamlEngine (request-body parsing with unrestricted SnakeYAML `new Yaml().load`)
candidates.trace: Attacker request -> PippoFilter/PippoServlet dispatch -> RouteDispatcher -> RouteContext/Request -> endpoint calls createEntityFromBody (DefaultRouteContext.java:193-196 -> Request.java:309) -> getBody()/getContentType() choose the raw body and the engine (Request.java:386-427 -> ContentTypeEngines.getContentTypeEngine, ContentTypeEngines.java:119-134) -> SnakeYamlInitializer-registered SnakeYamlEngine -> SnakeYamlEngine.fromString -> `new Yaml().load(content)` (SnakeYamlEngine.java:47-48) -> SnakeYAML 1.17 default Constructor resolves attacker-supplied YAML type tags and constructs the named classes / runs their side effects before the result is cast to the endpoint's entity type. Because object construction occurs inside `load`, the subsequent ClassCastException/PippoRuntimeException wrapping in Request.java:337-344 (or a 500 error page) does not undo the side effects already triggered by parsing.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and no exploit payload was executed or provided. The unsafe semantics of SnakeYAML's default `Yaml()`/`Constructor` for version 1.17 are asserted from library knowledge plus the pinned version in pippo-snakeyaml/pom.xml; the snakeyaml jar itself is not present in the snapshot, so the exact set of available gadget chains for a given application classpath was not verified. Whether a particular deployment reaches the sink depends on the optional module being present and on an endpoint using `@Body`/`createEntityFromBody`, neither of which can be confirmed from the library snapshot alone.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (unsafe object construction via YAML type tags; potential RCE)

coverage_summary: Scope: 387 model-visible source files, all under the assigned root; per get_source_scope there were 0 files excluded by size, sensitive-name, or symlink filters, and per get_relation_scope the P1 index covers 387/387 files (5574 edges, 2976 symbols, 142 facts) with no file hash mismatches; the index itself is syntactic/navigational only and was used solely to navigate, with every cited edge verified in source text. Files inspected include pippo-core (Request, Response, Application, Pippo, PippoFilter/PippoServlet, PippoSettings, Messages/Languages, DefaultErrorHandler, route/* including DefaultRouter, DefaultUriMatcher, resource/Directory/File/Classpath/Webjars handlers, CSRF/CORS/Language/TrailingSlash handlers, gzip/*, util/*, websocket/*), all content-type engines (snakeyaml, xstream, fastjson, gson, jackson, jaxb, csv), the session modules (base, cookie, jdbc, ehcache, xmemcached, etc.), pippo-controller, pippo-metrics, pippo-css, pippo-pac4j, representative template engines, server modules (jetty/tomcat/undertow/tjws settings and websocket filters), the archetype files, and the root/module POMs and CHANGELOG. The snapshot contains no test sources (0 files under any src/test path), so no repository tests were available to corroborate or refute any lead. Coverage is not line-exhaustive: PippoSettings (~1082 lines), the larger server/template engine classes, the remaining session-cache backends, and the metrics reporters were skimmed rather than read end-to-end, and no code was compiled, executed, or scanned.
limitations: Static review only: no build, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; the submitted candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

The SnakeYAML dependency jar is not vendored in the snapshot, so the library's default-constructor behaviour and the concrete gadget availability for a given application classpath were not verified from source in this run.

Reachability of the YAML sink depends on deployment choices (presence of the optional pippo-snakeyaml artifact, engine registration order, and an endpoint that deserializes request bodies) that cannot be settled from the library snapshot alone.

Runtime behaviour of the gzip response wrapper (whether bodies written via getWriter()/resource()/file() are actually dropped, and how containers treat duplicate Content-Length headers) could not be confirmed and remains an unverified secondary lead.
No coverage of external deployment artifacts (web.xml, container configuration, application code outside this repository) was possible, so end-to-end prerequisites for any candidate remain partial.

rejected_leads.lead: Default-on gzip response wrapping: Application.createRequestResponseFactory now returns GZipRequestResponseFactory (Application.java:281-284), which wraps any response when the client sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip` or even `*`, and GZipFilter/GZipRequestResponseFactory only use a substring check so `gzip;q=0` still gets compressed (GZipRequestResponseFactory.java:54-60). Bodies written through getWriter()/getOutputStream()/resource()/file() appear never to be flushed by GZipResponseWrapper.finish(), which is only invoked from Response.commit(CharSequence) (Response.java:1085-1108, 1135-1140), and GZipResponseStream.close() appends a second Content-Length/Content-Encoding via addHeader (GZipResponseStream.java:50-60).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible correctness/robustness defect (broken or empty responses for resource/file writer paths, spec-violating gzip selection, possible duplicate Content-Length) rather than a demonstrable attacker-controlled security impact; could not be confirmed without executing the container/response stack, so it was not submitted as the single candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SettingsHandler password masking uses a case-sensitive check: `name.contains(settingNamePasswordToken)` with the default token "password" (SettingsHandler.java:41-54, 80-90), so settings spelled with capitals are not masked — including the framework's own names `server.keystorePassword`/`server.truststorePassword` (PippoConstants.java:70-76); additionally settingNamePasswordToken stays null for the `SettingsHandler(boolean)` constructors, which would NPE on use.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness (secret disclosure to whoever can reach the settings route, plus an admin-route NPE), but it requires the application to expose SettingsHandler and to name secrets with a case variant of the token; impact and evidence are weaker than the deserialization candidate, and it was not confirmed that the casing nuance is a regression rather than an upstream design limitation.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded array allocation from indexed request parameter names in Request.initParameters: an attacker-supplied parameter name matching `name[<int>]` causes `new String[maxIndex + 1]` (Request.java:142-193), e.g. a very large index allocates a multi-gigabyte array or, at Integer.MAX_VALUE, a NegativeArraySizeException.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable in default configurations and a genuine memory-amplification/denial-of-service pattern (the code's own try/catch only covers NumberFormatException for out-of-int-range indexes), but impact is limited to OOM/500-level availability effects and it was not confirmed to be the intended target; kept as a secondary lead only.

rejected_leads.lead: Dev-mode error page reflects the request URI into HTML without encoding (DefaultErrorHandler.renderDirectly, DefaultErrorHandler.java:215-255; bindings at 264-295, including unescaped `message`/`requestUri` passed to templates).
rejected_leads.reason: Only active when the runtime mode is not PROD (dev/test), and exploitation also depends on browser encoding of `<`/`>` in the path and/or app error templates printing the values unescaped; treated as a hardening gap rather than the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal in static-resource handlers (FileResourceHandler.java:49-70, DirectoryHandler.java:150-186, ClasspathResourceHandler.isValidResourcePath / WebjarsResourceHandler.java:57-88).
rejected_leads.reason: Checked in detail: all three use normalize() plus element-wise Path.startsWith() containment (so `/opt/data-evil` does not pass for base `/opt/data`), ClasspathResourceHandler blocks `..` escapes, and DirectoryHandler only logs the rejected path. No traversal bypass was found, so no candidate was raised (this codebase did fix a ClasspathResourceHandler traversal previously, CHANGELOG.md:177).

rejected_leads.lead: CookieSessionDataStorage stores session state in a client cookie using the plain SerializationSessionDataTranscoder by default (CookieSessionDataStorage.java:41-71), and BaseEncryptor uses bare "AES" (ECB) with a caller-supplied key (BaseEncryptor.java:27-55).
rejected_leads.reason: Client-readable/tamperable session state and unauthenticated-ciphertext design weakness, but the deserialization whitelist (whitelist-serialization.txt via WhitelistObjectInputStream) blocks classical gadget RCE, tampering is largely self-directed, and the encrypted variant is the documented opt-in; judged lower-impact and largely a design/configuration issue.

summary: Reviewed the Pippo 1.12.0-SNAPSHOT multi-module source tree as a defensive source assessment (387 model-visible files; P1 index reports 387/387 indexed, index is navigation-only). I traced attacker-controlled request input into the ContentTypeEngine framework, the session/cookie machinery, static-resource handlers, CSRF/CORS handlers, the controller module, template/CSS modules, server modules, and build/config files. The single strongest candidate is the unrestricted SnakeYAML deserialization primitive exposed by the optional pippo-snakeyaml content-type engine: request bodies can be parsed with `new Yaml().load(...)` (SnakeYAML 1.17, no SafeConstructor / type restriction), which allows attacker-named YAML global tags to instantiate arbitrary classes and trigger side effects during parsing (classic CWE-502 unsafe deserialization, up to remote code execution). Neighbouring engines in the same codebase were explicitly hardened in this same dev cycle (XStream type whitelist for issue #454; Java serialization whitelist for issue #458; FastJSON bumped to 1.2.51), which makes the unguarded SnakeYAML engine the standout remaining unsafe deserializer. Rejected/unconfirmed leads (gzip response wrapping now on by default, SettingsHandler password-masking gaps, indexed-parameter array allocation DoS, dev-mode error-page URI reflection, and several path-traversal candidates) are listed below; no candidate was runtime-confirmed and no code was executed.
